provenance.source_title: Multi-criteria thermoeconomic and thermodynamic assessments of the desalination-integrated two-phase liquid-immersion data center cooling system

content.reading_plan: This is a technical research article combining a proposed engineering design, mathematical modeling, literature-based validation, economic assumptions, numerical results, and optimization. The prose is moderately dense, while the modeling sections require slower reading because definitions, equations, assumptions, and cited methods accumulate quickly. I will follow the document in order, generally taking a few paragraphs per step and shorter stretches around equations and tables. Readings of equations, tables, and figures will be identified as paraphrases. The closing reference list and appendices will also be included, without independently checking the cited works.

reading_path.location: PDF p. 1, Summary
reading_path.moves: States the problem, proposes a hybrid solution, specifies its scope, and previews numerical findings and an economic conclusion.

claims.text: The waste heat management of the data center cooling systems has a significant share in the energy-efficient operations of the data centers.
The proposed hybrid desalination–data-center cooling system is intended to reduce the cost drawback associated with cooling-system waste heat.
Two-phase liquid-immersion cooling is promising because of its high heat-flux removal performance, but research on its waste-heat management remains lacking.
The modeled system uses immersion-cooling waste heat to warm the feed of a direct contact membrane distillation module, examining cooling loads of 0.7–1.5 kW and membrane areas of 5–75 cm².
The hybrid design is assessed thermodynamically, economically, and thermoeconomically, with a design-specific exergy-cost matrix.
The maximum thermal and exergy efficiencies are found as 64.5% and 53.7%, respectively.
The daily distilled water rate can reach 6.13 kg at the highest cooling load and membrane area.
The hybrid system has higher capital and operating costs than stand-alone data-center cooling.
A payback period of 3.72 years is taken to establish that the proposed system is economically feasible for real applications.
The hybrid design's levelized product cost is 2.69–5.33 SGD/h.
The summary places the best optimization trade-off at a cooling load of 1.1 kW and membrane areas of 5.12–5.19 cm².

reading_path.meaning: The opening presents the work as a proposal supported by modeling and several assessment methods. Its feasibility language is affirmative, while its chosen cooling loads and membrane areas establish a small operating domain. These are preview claims; the supporting methods and results have not yet been developed.

reading_path.location: PDF pp. 1–2, Section 1, opening through conventional waste-heat recovery applications
reading_path.moves: Establishes the scale of the energy problem, explains why cooling is necessary, classifies cooling technologies, and introduces alternatives to rejecting heat to the environment.

reading_path.meaning: The introduction moves from a general demand problem to a specific opportunity: cooling is necessary, but environmental heat rejection is not the only possible endpoint. The numerical context supports the importance assigned to cooling rather than yet demonstrating the proposed hybrid.

reading_path.moves: Reviews a prior proposal, argues by analogy from other energy systems, invokes policy relevance, and identifies research gaps.

claims.text: Using data-center cooling waste heat for seawater desalination has previously been proposed, but without modeling and performance-assessment details.

support.text: Ebrahimi et al are identified as having proposed the use of waste heat or steam for desalination.

support.text: The authors enumerate desalination integrated with nuclear plants, marine energy and industry, solar energy, fuel cells and gas turbines, and thermoelectric coolers.

claims.text: The thermal energy generated by data-center waste-heat systems can supply sufficient energy to desalination units.
Combining cooling and desalination is critically important because it addresses SDGs 6 and 7 and belongs to the energy-water nexus.

support.text: The authors connect clean water and sanitation with affordable and clean energy, citing United Nations documents.

United Nations. Paris Agreement. 2015. https://unfccc.int/files/essential_background/convention/application/pdf/english_paris_agreement.pdf. Accessed March 23, 2020)

claims.text: A detailed study of this combined concept is missing, and system-scale waste-heat utilization studies of liquid-cooled data centers have not been widely performed, as far as the authors know.

support.text: The authors contrast this absence with a waste-heat utilization literature usually based on air-cooled systems.

reading_path.meaning: The proposed connection is motivated through precedents rather than presented as already demonstrated. The energy-water nexus adds a policy-oriented value frame to the earlier energy-cost frame, while the gap claim narrows the discussion toward liquid-cooled systems.

reading_path.location: PDF p. 2, Section 1, comparison of direct and indirect liquid cooling
reading_path.moves: Classifies alternatives, compares their advantages and drawbacks, and identifies a technology-specific academic gap.

claims.text: Liquid-cooled systems can remove higher heat fluxes than air-cooled systems because liquids have greater heat-removal performance.
Indirect liquid cooling is more established, but involves leakage potential in circulating pipework and layouts sized specifically for the required cooling load.

Direct cooling overcomes these challenges through dielectric-liquid contact with equipment surfaces, eliminating server- or rack-level liquid piping and allowing flexible adaptation to different cooling loads.
Direct cooling includes jet impingement, spray cooling, and two-phase liquid immersion, and can operate independently or alongside conventional air cooling.
Two-phase liquid immersion provides more uniform equipment-surface temperatures through latent-heat transfer.

support.text: The paragraph directs readers to four works for further details on liquid-cooled data centers.

claims.text: Despite their advantages, two-phase immersion systems lack widespread system-scale studies and academic thermal-management and economic-assessment research.

support.text: Submer Inc., GIGABYTE, 3M, and FUJITSU are named as companies undertaking system-scale work, distinguishing industrial activity from the identified academic gap.

reading_path.meaning: The comparison gives a reason for selecting immersion cooling rather than treating all liquid cooling as interchangeable. The framing is explicitly favorable to direct two-phase cooling, but the authors also distinguish technical promise from the availability of system-level assessment.

reading_path.location: PDF pp. 2–3, Section 1, authors' preceding studies and the low-load gap
reading_path.moves: Establishes continuity with prior work and qualifies the usefulness of an earlier waste-heat application.

claims.text: The authors previously developed a real-scale two-phase immersion setup and investigated transient performance up to 21 kW, obtaining satisfactory steady performance under real conditions.

support.text: Their earlier experimental system is offered as the basis for subsequent system-scale modeling.

citations.reference_entry: Wu C, Tong W, Kanbur BB, Duan F. Full-scale two-phase liquid immersion cooing data center system in tropical environment. Paper presented at: Proceedings of 2019 18th IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm); May 27-31, 2019; Las Vegas (NV), USA. doi:https://doi.org/10.1109/ITHERM.2019.8757316.

claims.text: Their subsequent mathematical model combined immersion cooling with a polymer electrolyte membrane fuel cell and indicated low-carbon electricity generation at a cooling load of nearly 6 kW.

support.text: The previous hybrid cooling–fuel-cell modeling study is cited.

citations.reference_entry: Kanbur BB, Wu C, Duan F. Combined heat and power generation via hybrid data center cooling-polymer electrolyte membrane fuel cell system. Int J Energy Res. 2020;44:4759-4772. https://doi.org/10.1002/er.5256.

claims.text: Below 6 kW, waste-heat utilization may not be efficient for low-carbon electricity generation or other familiar thermal processes, leaving a gap for more efficient and economical low-load immersion-cooling operation.

reading_path.meaning: The gap becomes more specific: the issue is not simply whether immersion cooling works, but what productive use can be made of its heat at lower loads. The authors preserve uncertainty here with 'may not,' rather than claiming that every alternative necessarily fails below 6 kW.

reading_path.location: PDF p. 3, Section 1, original-contribution list
reading_path.moves: Claims novelty, defines the intended contributions, and states the optimization objectives and design bounds.

claims.text: The proposed hybrid has not been investigated before and is the first use of two-phase liquid-immersion cooling for waste-heat utilization through desalination.
Routing cooling-system waste heat to DCMD permits clean-water production and offers a new alternative particularly suited to low cooling loads.
A newly constructed exergy-cost matrix may be useful for future waste-heat utilization studies of two-phase immersion systems.
The optimization aims to minimize distilled-water and system-product costs and maximize exergy efficiency, subject to cooling-load and membrane-area bounds of 0.7–1.5 kW and 5–75 cm².

reading_path.meaning: This contribution list restates the opening proposal while adding an explicit novelty claim and a prospective use for the cost matrix. The bounded design variables make clear that the claimed contribution is a particular modeled hybrid, not an unrestricted survey of desalination or cooling arrangements.

reading_path.location: PDF p. 3, Section 2, seawater inlet and immersion-cooling operation
reading_path.moves: Specifies boundary conditions, identifies equipment, explains the heat-transfer mechanism, and imposes a design limit.

claims.text: Stream 1 is seawater at 35 g/L salinity, 302.75 K, and 1 atm.

support.text: Standard seawater total dissolved solids and a Singapore seawater temperature source provide the inlet values.

World Sea Temperatures. Singapore sea temperatures. 2019. https://www.seatemperature.org/asia/singapore/singapore.htm. Accessed March 23, 2020.

claims.text: The selected feed pump is an EB120 by Euroflo; the customized server tank can handle up to 2 kW of released server heat and contains NOVEC 7100 dielectric liquid with a boiling temperature of 61°C.
Server power is assumed constant so that steady-state thermodynamic assessments can be performed.

support.text: A study of environmentally sustainable electronic cooling is cited alongside the constant-power assumption.

citations.reference_entry: Shah AJ, Patel CD. Designing environmentally sustainable electronic cooling systems using exergo-thermo-volumes. Int J Energy Res. 2009;33:1266-1277. https://doi.org/10.1002/er.1663.

claims.text: Server heat boils the dielectric bath; rising vapor condenses on cooler condenser pipes, returns to the bath, and transfers heat into the circulating coolant.

support.text: The authors identify the immersion setup as experimentally operated and verified in their previous work.

citations.reference_entry: Wu C, Tong W, Kanbur BB, Duan F. Full-scale two-phase liquid immersion cooing data center system in tropical environment. Paper presented at: Proceedings of 2019 18th IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm); May 27-31, 2019; Las Vegas (NV), USA. doi:https://doi.org/10.1109/ITHERM.2019.8757316.

claims.text: Seawater is used as that coolant, warming before entering DCMD; its outlet temperature must remain below the dielectric boiling temperature, with a selected minimum temperature difference of 3 K.

reading_path.meaning: The proposal now becomes a physically specified sequence. The seawater is not immersed with the servers: it flows through condenser pipes and receives heat from dielectric vapor. The 3 K margin introduces a practical constraint connecting the cooling medium to the available desalination temperature.

reading_path.location: PDF p. 3, Section 2, DCMD operation and stream changes
reading_path.moves: Defines the desalination arrangement and explains how the temperature difference produces separation.

claims.text: DCMD is described as the oldest membrane-distillation technique, using a membrane interface without an air-gap or conductive-material interface.

support.text: A membrane-distillation configuration comparison is cited for this description.

citations.reference_entry: Swaminathan J, Chung HW, Warsinger DM, Lienhard VJH. Membrane distillation model based on heat exchanger theory and configuration comparison. Appl Energy. 2016;184:491-505. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apenergy.2016.09.090.

claims.text: The permeate inlet is pumped from stream 5, initially at 293.15 K, to stream 6 on the opposite side of the membrane.
The feed–permeate temperature difference creates a vapor-pressure difference, driving heat and mass transport through a hydrophobic membrane that blocks liquid passage but allows vapor transfer.
Separation reduces the feed-side outlet mass flow at stream 4 relative to stream 3 and increases the permeate-side outlet mass flow at stream 7 relative to stream 6.

reading_path.meaning: The system description connects recovered heat to the separation mechanism. Changes in outlet mass flow are introduced as consequences of vapor transport, establishing quantities that will later define water production and membrane flux.

reading_path.location: PDF p. 4, Section 2 assumptions; Figures 1–2; opening of Section 3
reading_path.moves: States simplifying assumptions and numerical inputs, supplies a system schematic, and outlines the calculation sequence.

claims.text: The model assumes steady-state operation, neglects membrane fouling, and treats the tank, DCMD module, and piping as insulated with no heat loss.

support.text: The piping assumption is justified by earlier experimental observations of very small heat losses from insulated pipes at small liquid-to-ambient temperature differences.

citations.reference_entry: Wu C, Tong W, Kanbur BB, Duan F. Full-scale two-phase liquid immersion cooing data center system in tropical environment. Paper presented at: Proceedings of 2019 18th IEEE Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems (ITherm); May 27-31, 2019; Las Vegas (NV), USA. doi:https://doi.org/10.1109/ITHERM.2019.8757316.

claims.text: Corrosion and salt deposition are neglected both in performance calculations and in considering pipeline damage.
Feed and permeate inlet velocities are 1.85 and 2.92 m/s, respectively, both with a hydraulic diameter of 0.003 m.

support.text: DCMD heat- and mass-transfer characteristics are adopted from Reference 31.

citations.reference_entry: Termpiyakul P, Jiraratananon R, Srisurichan S. Heat and mass transfer characteristics of a direct contact membrane distillation process for desalination. Desalination. 2005;177:133-141. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.desal.2004.11.019.

claims.text: The PVDF membrane has thickness 126 μm, thermal conductivity 0.41 W/mK, porosity 0.75, and pore size 0.22 μm.

support.text: These membrane properties are also taken from Reference 31.

citations.reference_entry: Termpiyakul P, Jiraratananon R, Srisurichan S. Heat and mass transfer characteristics of a direct contact membrane distillation process for desalination. Desalination. 2005;177:133-141. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.desal.2004.11.019.

claims.text: The thermodynamic reference state is 293.15 K and 1 atm.
Figure 1 shows separate seawater and permeate paths linked by the membrane, with electrical inputs to the two pumps and seawater passing first through the immersion-tank condenser.

Figure 2 organizes the method from fluid-property and pump calculations through iterative membrane calculations, energy and exergy assessments, economic analysis, an exergy-cost matrix, and genetic-algorithm optimization.

reading_path.meaning: These assumptions define what the subsequent results do and do not represent. The figures consolidate the preceding physical description and introduce a staged computational workflow; they do not depict a newly tested integrated prototype.

reading_path.location: PDF p. 5, Section 3.1, water and seawater properties, Equations (1)–(4)
reading_path.moves: Defines the property model and distinguishes the two working fluids.

claims.text: The energy model uses enthalpy-based assessment, with seawater on the feed side and water on the permeate side requiring different thermophysical-property correlations.

support.text: The authors select the correlations of Sharqawy et al; Equations (1)–(4) give water enthalpy and density and salinity-dependent seawater enthalpy and density.

citations.reference_entry: Sharqawy MH, Lienhard VJH, Zubair SM. Thermophysical properties of seawater: a review of existing correlations and data. Desalin Water Treat. 2010;16:354-380. https://doi.org/10.5004/dwt.2010.1079.

claims.text: A stream's enthalpy rate is calculated by multiplying its specific enthalpy by its mass flow rate; mass flow follows from volume flow and density, with volume flow obtained using velocity and hydraulic diameter.
Equation (3) represents seawater enthalpy as water enthalpy plus terms involving salinity, salinity to the three-halves power, and salinity squared; Appendix A supplies the coefficients.
Equation (4) gives the seawater-density correlation, with its coefficients supplied in Appendix B; these calculations determine inlet enthalpy rates for streams 1 and 5.

reading_path.meaning: The analysis begins with properties rather than aggregate efficiencies. Separating water from seawater preserves the distinction already established between the two sides of the membrane, and the appendices are introduced as part of the model's specification.

reading_path.location: PDF pp. 5–6, Section 3.1, Equations (5)–(11)
reading_path.moves: Applies component energy balances and constructs the convective parts of the membrane heat-transfer model.

claims.text: Equations (5) and (6) add feed- and permeate-pump work to their inlet enthalpy rates; Equation (7) adds the data-center heat rate to stream 2 to obtain stream 3.
The enthalpy–temperature relationship permits calculation of the heated seawater temperature T3 before solving the DCMD model.
Heat flows from the hotter feed through the membrane to the permeate, requiring separate feed-side, membrane, and permeate-side heat-flux expressions.
Equations (8) and (9) express the feed- and permeate-side convective heat fluxes using their heat-transfer coefficients and fluid-to-membrane-surface temperature differences.

The assumed transport direction requires feed-fluid temperature to exceed feed membrane-surface temperature, which exceeds permeate membrane-surface temperature, which exceeds permeate-fluid temperature.

Equation (10) determines convective coefficients from Nusselt number, fluid thermal conductivity, and hydraulic diameter; Equation (11) uses a Dittus–Boelter correlation involving Reynolds number, Prandtl number, and channel dimensions.

support.text: Reference 31 supplies the cited convection correlation.

citations.reference_entry: Termpiyakul P, Jiraratananon R, Srisurichan S. Heat and mass transfer characteristics of a direct contact membrane distillation process for desalination. Desalination. 2005;177:133-141. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.desal.2004.11.019.

reading_path.meaning: The equations connect the components in the same order as the physical system. The membrane-surface temperatures are distinguished from bulk-fluid temperatures, making clear why the inlet temperatures alone are not enough to calculate transport.

reading_path.location: PDF p. 6, Section 3.1, membrane transport, Equations (12)–(14)
reading_path.moves: Decomposes heat transfer, defines mass flux, compares modeling alternatives, and imposes a no-loss balance.

claims.text: Equation (12) divides membrane heat flux into latent heat carried by vapor and conductive heat transfer through the membrane.
The enthalpy-of-vaporization correlation is adopted experimentally, although a physical model could instead be constructed using nonequilibrium thermodynamics and the Clausius–Clapeyron equation.

support.text: Reference 31 supplies the adopted correlation, while Luo and Lior are cited for the alternative physical formulation.

citations.reference_entry: Termpiyakul P, Jiraratananon R, Srisurichan S. Heat and mass transfer characteristics of a direct contact membrane distillation process for desalination. Desalination. 2005;177:133-141. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.desal.2004.11.019.
Luo A, Lior N. Critical review of membrane distillation performance criteria. Desalin Water Treat. 2016;57:20093–20140. https://doi.org/10.1080/19443994.2016.1152637.

claims.text: Equation (13) defines membrane mass flux as either the feed-side mass-flow decrease or permeate-side mass-flow increase divided by membrane area.

Mass flux can alternatively be calculated from permeability and vapor-pressure difference or from nonequilibrium transport and membrane characteristics, but experimentally measured membrane characteristics may add uncertainty.

support.text: The authors identify porosity, average pore diameter, average membrane temperature, and membrane thickness among the relevant characteristics and cite membrane-characterization work.

citations.reference_entry: Tanis Kanbur MB, Peinador RI, Hu X, Calvo JI, Chew JW. Membrane characterization via evapoporometry (EP) and liquid-liquid displacement porosimetry (LLDP) techniques. J Membr Sci. 2019;586:248-258. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.memsci.2019.05.077.
Luo A, Lior N. Critical review of membrane distillation performance criteria. Desalin Water Treat. 2016;57:20093–20140. https://doi.org/10.1080/19443994.2016.1152637.

claims.text: Using mass-flow rates is an easier way to calculate mass flux, especially for experimental setups.
With surface heat loss neglected, Equation (14) equates feed-side, membrane, and permeate-side heat fluxes.

reading_path.meaning: The authors distinguish productive latent transfer from conduction and explain why they prefer a mass-flow representation of flux. The equality of the three heat fluxes supplies the condition around which the next iterative solution is organized.

reading_path.location: PDF p. 6, Section 3.1, iterative solution and Equations (15)–(17)
reading_path.moves: Describes the numerical procedure, qualifies its scale of applicability, and introduces entropy calculations.

claims.text: The DCMD equations require iteration because bulk inlet temperatures are known but the two membrane-surface temperatures are unknown and affect the transport parameters.

support.text: The procedure starts with an estimated feed-side membrane temperature and iterates until the heat-flux equality in Equation (14) is achieved.

claims.text: Feed- and permeate-side Prandtl numbers are calculated separately at the mean of the local bulk-fluid and membrane-surface temperatures.

support.text: Reference 31 is cited for the mean-temperature treatment.

citations.reference_entry: Termpiyakul P, Jiraratananon R, Srisurichan S. Heat and mass transfer characteristics of a direct contact membrane distillation process for desalination. Desalination. 2005;177:133-141. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.desal.2004.11.019.

claims.text: Mean-temperature evaluation is reasonable for small DCMD setups but must be replaced by dynamic observation of temperature gradients in large commercial systems, where those gradients may be nonlinear.
Equation (15) balances feed-side enthalpy reduction with permeate-side enthalpy increase and membrane heat flux multiplied by area, enabling outlet-state calculations for streams 4 and 7.

support.text: Luo and Lior are cited for further DCMD modeling and energy-balance details.

citations.reference_entry: Luo A, Lior N. Critical review of membrane distillation performance criteria. Desalin Water Treat. 2016;57:20093–20140. https://doi.org/10.1080/19443994.2016.1152637.

claims.text: Equations (16) and (17) give separate water and seawater entropy correlations, with seawater coefficients deferred to Appendix C.

support.text: The entropy correlations are attributed to Sharqawy et al.

citations.reference_entry: Sharqawy MH, Lienhard VJH, Zubair SM. Thermophysical properties of seawater: a review of existing correlations and data. Desalin Water Treat. 2010;16:354-380. https://doi.org/10.5004/dwt.2010.1079.

reading_path.meaning: The method now has an explicit solution sequence rather than just a collection of equations. The scale qualification matters: the authors do not present the small-system temperature treatment as automatically adequate for commercial-scale modeling.

reading_path.location: PDF pp. 6–7, Section 3.1, exergy framework, Equations (18)–(19)
reading_path.moves: Introduces second-law accounting, defines stream exergy, and explains included and excluded terms.

claims.text: Exergy assessments reveal second-law destruction and loss terms that energy assessments cannot provide.
Equation (18) defines specific stream exergy from enthalpy and entropy departures from the reference state; multiplication by mass flow gives the stream exergy rate.

support.text: The specific-exergy expression is accompanied by Reference 35.

citations.reference_entry: Kanbur BB, Xiang L, Dubey S, Choo FH, Duan F. A micro cogeneration system with LNG cold utilization-part 2: exergy analyses. Energy Procedia. 2017;105:1910-1917. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.egypro.2017.03.559.

claims.text: Chemical exergy is omitted because the authors state that there is no change in the chemical components of the streams.

claims.text: Future demonstration should investigate system limitations, alternative membrane characteristics, distillation techniques, and dielectric liquids.
Corrosion and salt deposition on condenser pipes should be tested experimentally.
A second research direction is larger-scale operation to determine its thermodynamic and thermoeconomic effects, including corrosion and salt-deposition investigations at that scale.

reading_path.meaning: The article closes its argument with a research program rather than a claim that deployment has already occurred. Effects omitted from the model, especially corrosion and salt deposition, return explicitly as experimental questions.

reading_path.moves: Defines notation, clarifies units and abbreviations, and acknowledges research support.

claims.text: The nomenclature distinguishes unit cost, annual cost, and levelized cost, listing their units respectively as $/kJ, $, and $/s or $/h.
The notation list identifies membrane flux in kg/m²s, gain output and performance ratios in percent, and sustainability index as dimensionless.
The acknowledgments attribute funding support to a joint project of Nanyang Technological University and Singapore's Defense, Science & Technology Agency.

reading_path.meaning: The supporting matter helps distinguish similarly named quantities used throughout the model, particularly the different cost measures. It adds no new performance evidence or integrated-system validation.

support.text: Equations (A1)–(A3) provide cubic temperature polynomials for the enthalpy coefficients.
